paragraphs: Swamiji once told a fable about the Buddha. When Buddha was born, so the story goes, he was so pure that anyone who even glimpsed his face from afar gave up ritual religion, became a monk and was saved.

This alarmed the gods. Most of them lived on ceremonial sacrifices, and now the offerings had stopped. Starving and losing their power, they met and agreed that, one way or another, this man had to be brought down. He was simply too pure for them to survive.

So they approached Buddha with a request. They were planning a great sacrifice with an enormous fire, they said, and had searched the whole world for a spot pure enough to light it on. At last they had found one: his chest. Would he lie down and let them build the fire there? Buddha calmly agreed.

The gods heaped the fire high on his breast and assumed he was dead. But he was not. Panicking, they rained blows on him. Nothing worked; he could not be killed. Then a voice spoke from beneath the fire, asking why they were wasting their efforts. They confessed their fear: whoever looked at him was purified and saved, and no one would worship them anymore. The reply came: their effort was useless, "because purity can never be killed."
Swamiji pointed out that this fable was actually written by Buddha's opponents. Yet the only fault they could find in him was that he taught purity too well.
learn: Genuine goodness can be attacked, mocked or resented, but it can't be destroyed. When even your critics can only complain that you are too honest or too kind, you are on the right track.
